pos: n. (the southernmost of the three Waldensian valleys of Piedmont, running from Torre Pellice up to Bobbio)
etymology: Italian Val Pellice, the valley of the river Pellice, a name of Ligurian or pre-Roman origin; the English works call it the Valley of Luserna from the plain below it.
biblical_def: The Val Pellice is the southernmost and largest of the three valleys of the Cottian Alps which held the Waldensian church, running westward from the Piedmontese plain past Torre Pellice and Villar to Bobbio and the French frontier, with the lateral valley of Angrogna opening to the north. For something over four hundred years before the Reformation these valleys held a people who had their own preachers, their own vernacular Scriptures and their own quarrel with Rome, and who in 1532 at the synod of Chanforan in Angrogna resolved to join themselves to the Reformed churches and to pay for the printing of a French Bible. From that decision the valley's history is a chronicle of sieges, edicts, and returns: the campaigns of 1560 and 1561, the edict of 1655 and the Easter massacre that followed it, the expulsion of 1686 after Louis the Fourteenth pressed his nephew at Turin, and the return of 1689 under Henri Arnaud. The population of the whole valley was never large—a few thousand families on steep ground—and it survived every attempt to end it. The dictionary enters the Val Pellice because the plainest fact about it is a geographical one with a doctrinal use: a church with almost no wealth and no army held a confession for five centuries in a place too poor to be worth keeping and too steep to be easily taken.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a valley as a hollow between hills; a vale as a tract of low ground between hills; and a fastness as a strong hold, a place not easily forced.
webster_full: VALLEY, n. [Fr. vallee.] A hollow or low tract of land between hills or mountains; a vale.
VALE, n. [L. vallis.] A tract of low ground, or of land between hills; a valley; used chiefly in poetry.
FASTNESS, n. [Sax. fastnes.] A strong hold; a fortress or fort; a place not easily forced; a place of security.
ALPINE, adj. [L. alpinus.] Pertaining to the Alps or to any high mountain; very high; elevated.
REMNANT, n. [L. remanens.] That which is left after a part is taken, destroyed or lost; a residue; a small remaining number.

corruption_summary: The largest of the three Waldensian valleys of Piedmont, which held its confession through the massacres of 1560, 1655 and the expulsion of 1686.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the romance of the valleys, which began with the seventeenth-century Protestant histories and is still printed: a pure apostolic church hidden in the Alps from the days of the apostles, untouched by the corruptions of the Middle Ages. It is not true. The Waldensians were a medieval movement with a datable origin, they held several doctrines the Reformation afterwards corrected, and the synod of 1532 was a real change of position and not a recognition of an identity.

The principle to recover is the doctrine of the remnant, which is the honest and better version of the romance. “Even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace” (Rom 11:5) does not require the remnant to be perfect, ancient or numerous; it requires it to be God's. “they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth” (Heb 11:38) is the apostle's own description, and the valleys fit it without any need of a legend.

pos: n. (the highest and most isolated of the three Waldensian valleys of Piedmont, with Prali at its head)
etymology: Italian Val Germanasca, the valley of the Germanasca torrent, from a pre-Roman root; the French works call it the Val Saint-Martin.
biblical_def: The Val Germanasca is the uppermost of the three Waldensian valleys, a narrow trench of the Cottian Alps opening from the Chisone above Perosa and climbing to Prali under the watershed, with the hamlets of Massello, Rodoretto and Salza on its flanks. It was the poorest and the least accessible of the three, which made it the last refuge in every persecution and the hardest ground for a church to serve: its congregations lay hours apart on footpaths that were shut by snow for months, its pastors travelled on foot between them, and its people lived by rye, chestnuts, goats and the talc quarries. In the great persecutions the valley was the place the others fled to, and in the expulsion of 1686 it was cleared like the rest. The dictionary enters it because the ministry of such a valley is the plainest possible test of what a pastor is for. There was no society to be gained, no stipend worth the name, and no prospect of advancement; what there was to do was to walk up a mountain in winter to preach to forty people and to catechise their children. A church which cannot staff a place like the Val Germanasca will not hold the places that are easier either, because the men who will not go there are the men who went into the ministry for something else.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a hamlet as a small village; to catechise as to instruct by question and answer; and a stipend as settled pay for services.
webster_full: HAMLET, n. [Sax. ham, a house.] A small village; a little cluster of houses in the country.
CATECHISE, v.t. [Gr. to instruct by word of mouth.] To instruct by asking questions and correcting the answers; to question as to religious belief.
STIPEND, n. [L. stipendium.] Settled pay or compensation for services, whether daily or monthly wages or an annual salary.
ISOLATED, adj. [It. isolato.] Standing detached from others of a like kind; placed by itself; separated.
FOOTPATH, n. A narrow path or way for foot passengers only.

corruption_summary: The highest and poorest Waldensian valley, the last refuge in every persecution, whose congregations lay hours apart on footpaths shut by snow.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live corruption is the career ministry: men entering the pastorate as a profession with a ladder in it, so that the small, cold, distant and poor congregations are staffed by whoever could not get anything better, and are understood by everybody to be a stage. The apostolic requirement is the opposite and is stated without any allowance: “not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind” (1Pe 5:2). A valley like this exposes the motive because it offers nothing else.

The principle to recover is the sufficiency of the charge itself. “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2) is the whole of the commission, and it says nothing about the size of the congregation. The dictionary holds that the health of a church may be measured fairly accurately by how its smallest and most inconvenient congregations are served, and that this is a measurement most denominations avoid taking.

pos: n. (Waldensian village of the Val Pellice between Torre Pellice and Bobbio)
etymology: Italian Villar, from Late Latin villare, a farmstead or hamlet; Pellice from the river, distinguishing it from the other Villars of Piedmont.
biblical_def: Villar Pellice is the middle village of the Val Pellice, between Torre at the valley mouth and Bobbio at its head, and it has been a Waldensian parish continuously since before the Reformation. Its history is the valley's in small: the men of Villar were at Chanforan in 1532; the village was burned and its people driven to the heights in the campaigns of the 1560s and again in the persecution of 1655; it was emptied in the expulsion of 1686 and resettled after the return of 1689; and through all of it the parish kept its register, its consistory and its school. That last point is the dictionary's reason for the entry. The Waldensian valleys maintained, from well before it was common anywhere in Europe, a system of hamlet schools—the little schools held through the winter months in the high quarters when the children could not get down to the village—so that a people living on terraced rye-fields in the Alps was literate when the peasantry of the plains below was not. They were literate because the church required it, and the church required it because a man is to read the Scriptures for himself.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a village as a small assemblage of houses; a school as a place of instruction; and literate as instructed in learning, able to read.
webster_full: VILLAGE, n. [L. villa.] A small assemblage of houses, less than a town or city, and inhabited chiefly by farmers and laborers.
SCHOOL, n. A place or house in which persons are instructed in arts, science, languages or any species of learning.
LITERATE, adj. [L. literatus.] Learned; lettered; instructed in learning and science; able to read.
WINTER, n. [Sax. winter.] The cold season of the year; in northern latitudes, the season when the sun is most distant.
TERRACE, n. [Fr. terrasse.] A raised level space or platform of earth, supported on one or more sides by a wall.

corruption_summary: Middle village of the Val Pellice, burned and resettled repeatedly, which kept its register, consistory and winter hamlet schools throughout.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption that a people's literacy is a function of its wealth. The Waldensian valleys were among the poorest inhabited places in western Europe and among the most literate, and the reason was doctrinal rather than economic: a church which holds that every man must read the Scriptures for himself will teach reading or stop believing its own doctrine. The plains below were richer and could not read.

The principle to recover is in the apostle's plain imperative, “Search the scriptures” (Joh 5:39), which presupposes a reader. The dictionary holds that the teaching of reading is a church's duty where the state does not do it, that the winter schools of these hamlets are the model, and that the obligation falls first on parents: “Train up a child in the way he should go” (Pro 22:6) is addressed to a household before it is addressed to an institution.

pos: n. (hamlet at the head of the Angrogna valley in Piedmont; traditionally the training place of the Waldensian barbes)
etymology: Italian Pra del Torno, the meadow of the torrent or of the turning, from prato, a meadow; the hamlet lies in a basin at the head of the gorge.
biblical_def: Pra del Torno is a cluster of houses in a high basin at the head of the Angrogna valley, reached by a gorge so narrow that for centuries a handful of men could hold it, and the Waldensian tradition made it the place where the barbes were trained. The barbes—the word is the local dialect for uncle, used as the title of the Waldensian preachers—were itinerants: they went out two by two, often disguised as pedlars, carrying portions of Scripture in the vernacular, and travelled a circuit which reached from Provence and Dauphine through Piedmont into Calabria and as far as Bohemia and the German lands. Their training is said to have been given here over several years, chiefly in the memorising of large parts of the Scriptures in the Romance tongue, since a man who could be searched could not safely carry a book. The later Protestant writers called the place the school or the university of the barbes, which is more than the evidence will carry; what the evidence shows is a remote hamlet, a tradition of training, and a ministry that demonstrably worked. The dictionary enters Pra del Torno for the method. Men who expected to be searched committed the Scriptures to memory, and a church under the same expectation would do well to consider it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines itinerant as travelling about, not settled; to memorize as to commit to memory; and a pedlar as one who travels about the country selling small wares.
webster_full: ITINERANT, adj. Passing or traveling about a country; wandering; not settled; applied to preachers who travel a circuit.
MEMORIZE, v.t. To cause to be remembered; to commit to memory; to record.
PEDLAR, n. A petty dealer who travels about the country with a pack of goods for sale; a hawker.
DISGUISE, v.t. To conceal by an unusual dress, or by a counterfeit appearance; to hide by a false show.
GORGE, n. [Fr. gorge, the throat.] A narrow passage between hills or mountains; a defile.

corruption_summary: Remote Angrogna hamlet where the Waldensian barbes were trained, chiefly by committing large parts of Scripture in the vernacular to memory.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the inflation of the tradition. There was no university at Pra del Torno; the seventeenth-century Protestant historians, needing an ancient and respectable pedigree for the Waldensian church, gave a hamlet one. The dictionary separates the claim from the fact, keeps the fact, and notes that the claim has done the Waldensian cause harm, since a case supported by an exaggeration is easily dismissed along with it.

The principle to recover is the one in the apostle's word to the Colossians: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom” (Col 3:16). The barbes took it literally because they had to. A church which possesses printed Bibles in abundance and whose members can quote almost none of it has a weakness it has not yet had occasion to discover, and the dictionary holds that systematic memorising of Scripture is a duty and not a childhood exercise.

pos: n. (Scipione Lentolo, c. 1525–1599, Neapolitan evangelical, pastor in the Waldensian valleys and historian of their persecutions)
etymology: Lentolo, an Italian surname, probably from Latin lentulus, somewhat slow; Scipione, from the Roman Scipio, a staff.
biblical_def: Scipione Lentolo was a Neapolitan who had been a Carmelite and who, converted to the evangelical faith, left Italy and was ordained in the Reformed church. From 1559 he served as a pastor in the Waldensian valleys of Piedmont, and he was there through the campaigns of 1560 and 1561 in which the Duke of Savoy's forces attempted to destroy the valley churches and failed, so that the peace of Cavour granted the Waldensians a limited toleration. Lentolo wrote the history of that persecution from his own knowledge and from the testimony of those who had survived it, a work which remained the foundation of all later Waldensian historiography. He was afterwards pastor at Chiavenna in the Valtellina, where he served the Italian evangelical refugees for thirty years, defended the Reformed doctrine against the antitrinitarians who had followed them north, and died in 1599. The dictionary enters him because he is the first instance of what the Waldensian church would need repeatedly: a man of the plains, trained and literate, who came up into the valleys, served them, and then wrote down what had happened to them in a form the rest of Europe could read.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a historian as a writer of history; toleration as the allowance of religious opinions not approved; and testimony as a solemn declaration establishing a fact.
webster_full: HISTORIAN, n. [L. historicus.] A writer or compiler of history; one who relates or records events in the order of time.
TOLERATION, n. The allowance of that which is not wholly approved; the allowance of religious opinions and modes of worship in a state.
TESTIMONY, n. A solemn declaration or affirmation made for the purpose of establishing or proving some fact.
REFUGEE, n. One who flies to a shelter or place of safety; one who flees from persecution to a foreign country.
CHRONICLE, n. [Gr. time.] A history or account of events in the order of time; a register.

corruption_summary: Neapolitan evangelical who pastored the Waldensian valleys through the campaigns of 1560 and wrote the history of the persecution from the survivors' testimony.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live question is the reliability of a martyrology written by a participant, and the dictionary will not pretend it is not a question. Lentolo was a pastor of the people he wrote about, he wrote to be read in Geneva and Zurich where help was wanted, and his numbers and his adjectives must be read with that in mind. What he does supply, and what no later account could, is the names, the villages, the dates and the testimony of people he knew; and a history with a purpose is not for that reason a history with no facts.

The principle to recover is the duty to write. “Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables” (Hab 2:2) was obeyed for the Waldensians by a Neapolitan refugee who had no obligation to them beyond the gospel. “I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God” (Rev 6:9) names the only register that finally matters; the registers men keep are a small imitation of it and are worth keeping for that reason.

pos: n. (Jean Leger, 1615–c. 1675, Waldensian pastor and moderator, eyewitness and historian of the Piedmontese Easter of 1655)
etymology: Leger, French, from the Germanic Leodegar, people-spear; Jean, the French form of John, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious.
biblical_def: Jean Leger was a Waldensian of the valleys, trained at Geneva, pastor at Villar and then at San Giovanni, and moderator of the Waldensian church in the years of its worst trial. In January 1655 the court at Turin ordered the Waldensians of the lower valleys to quit their homes in the depth of winter or conform to Rome, and when they petitioned instead, an army was sent in; the killing which followed in April, in Torre, Villar, Bobbio, Angrogna and the hamlets, is the event the Protestant world called the Piedmontese Easter. Leger was in it, lost his house, gathered the survivors' depositions, and carried the case abroad; the massacre produced Cromwell's intervention and collection in England, Milton's sonnet, and the Swiss and Dutch embassies which obtained the patent of Pinerolo. Driven out of Piedmont with a price on him, Leger settled in the Netherlands and published in 1669 his general history of the evangelical churches of the valleys—a folio of documents, depositions, engravings and narrative which is the chief source for the whole episode. The dictionary enters him for the work: a pastor who answered a massacre by collecting evidence.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a deposition as testimony reduced to writing; a moderator as one who presides over an assembly; and a massacre as the murder of many persons indiscriminately.
webster_full: DEPOSITION, n. [L. depositio.] The act of giving testimony under oath; the testimony given, reduced to writing and attested.
MODERATOR, n. One who presides over an assembly or meeting to preserve order; the president of a synod or presbytery.
MASSACRE, n. [Fr.] The murder of an individual, or the slaughter of numbers of human beings, with cruelty or without necessity.
PATENT, n. [L. patens, open.] A writ or open letter from a sovereign, granting a right or privilege.
ENGRAVING, n. The act or art of cutting figures on metal or wood; a print taken from an engraved plate.

corruption_summary: Waldensian moderator and eyewitness of the massacre of 1655, who gathered the depositions and published the general history of the valley churches in 1669.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the religious massacre carried out under colour of an order of removal. The Turin edict of January 1655 did not command killing; it commanded a people to leave their houses in winter or change their religion, and sent soldiers to see it done. That is the usual form: a legal instrument whose execution is foreseeably murderous, and a government which afterwards disclaims the manner while keeping the result. The dictionary names it as persecution and names the court that ordered it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one Leger acted on. “Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them” (Heb 13:3) was obeyed in 1655 at a European scale—English collections, Swiss and Dutch embassies, a patent obtained—and it worked because one man had taken depositions. Sympathy without evidence achieves nothing; the church that wants to help the persecuted must first find out exactly what happened, to whom, on what date, and get it written down.

pos: n. (village of the Luberon in Provence; destroyed with its Waldensian population in the massacre of 1545)
etymology: Provençal Merindol, from a pre-Latin root with the Occitan diminutive; the village stands on the north slope of the Luberon above the Durance.
biblical_def: Merindol was a village of Waldensian settlers in the Luberon hills of Provence, part of a colony which had come down from the Alpine valleys in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries to farm land left empty by plague and war. In 1540 the Parlement of Aix issued a decree against the inhabitants of Merindol, condemning them in their absence and ordering the village razed and its people seized. For five years the decree was suspended while the king was petitioned. In April 1545 it was executed. The baron of Oppede, as president of the Parlement, led a force of royal and papal troops through the Luberon; Merindol and Cabrieres were destroyed with some twenty other villages and hamlets, men were killed in the field and in the churches where they had taken refuge, women and children died with them, and a number of the survivors were sent to the galleys. The estimates of the dead run into the thousands. The dictionary enters Merindol because this is the largest single massacre of Protestants in France before the wars of religion, it was carried out by a court of law in execution of its own judgment, and it is very largely forgotten.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a decree as a judicial decision or order; to raze as to demolish, to level with the ground; and a parlement as a supreme court of judicature in France.
webster_full: DECREE, n. [L. decretum.] Judicial decision, or determination of a litigated cause; an order, edict or law made by a superior.
RAZE, v.t. [L. rado.] To subvert from the foundation; to overthrow; to destroy; to level with the ground.

corruption_summary: Provençal Waldensian village destroyed in April 1545, with Cabrieres and some twenty others, in execution of a decree of the Parlement of Aix.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is judicial murder on a national scale, and the dictionary insists on the judicial part. The destruction of the Luberon villages was not a riot, a pogrom or a frontier atrocity. It was the enforcement of a sentence passed in 1540 by a court of record, led in person by that court's president, and the court afterwards defended its act as law. “yea, the time cometh, that whosoever killeth you will think that he doeth God service” (Joh 16:2) describes the state of mind exactly, and the men who held it were magistrates and not fanatics.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the obligation to remember what is inconvenient to remember. The Luberon massacre is poorly known in comparison with Saint Bartholomew, partly because its victims were poor hill farmers with no noble patrons and no historian of their own, and partly because France afterwards had reasons not to dwell on it. The dictionary holds that the church's roll of its martyrs should be kept without regard to their rank, and that the obscure dead are exactly the ones a register is for.

pos: n. (village of the Luberon in Provence, destroyed with Merindol in the massacre of April 1545)
etymology: Provençal Cabrières, from Late Latin capraria, a goat-pasture, from capra, a goat.
biblical_def: Cabrieres was the second of the two Waldensian villages of Provence named in the Parlement of Aix's decree, and it was the place where the killing of April 1545 was worst. The village had a wall and a tower and some of its men attempted a defence; when it was taken, on terms according to the Protestant accounts, the terms were not kept. Men who had surrendered were killed, a number of people who had taken refuge in the church were killed there, and others were burned in a barn. With Merindol and the surrounding hamlets the destruction of Cabrieres ended the Waldensian presence in Provence as a distinct community, though families survived and were absorbed into the Reformed churches of the region in the following decades. The baron of Oppede was later prosecuted in Paris for the conduct of the campaign and was acquitted. The dictionary enters Cabrieres beside Merindol because the pair of them make a single point which no amount of later legal process altered: a surrender taken and then dishonoured, and an acquittal, are the ordinary end of a persecution conducted by a government, and the people who died had no remedy in this world at all.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a surrender as the yielding of a town to an enemy; faith as fidelity, the observance of a promise; and an acquittal as a setting free from a charge.
webster_full: SURRENDER, n. The act of yielding or resigning one's person or the possession of something into the power of another; the yielding of a town to an enemy.
FAITH, n. [L. fides.] Fidelity; the observance of a promise or a treaty; the keeping of one's word.
ACQUITTAL, n. A judicial setting free, or deliverance from the charge of an offense, as by verdict of a jury or sentence of a court.
QUARTER, n. In war, the sparing of the life of a prisoner or of an enemy who yields; mercy granted by a conqueror.
PERFIDY, n. [L. perfidia.] The act of violating faith or allegiance; treachery; the violation of a trust reposed.

corruption_summary: Provençal Waldensian village taken and destroyed in April 1545, where a surrender was dishonoured and the commander was later acquitted.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the breaking of faith with a people who have laid down their arms. It is a crime by the law of nations as well as by the law of God, and the men who did it at Cabrieres were acting under a judicial decree and were acquitted of the manner of its execution. The dictionary names it for what it is and declines the excuse that the age was violent; the age also knew the difference, which is why the baron was prosecuted at all, and why the acquittal was resented.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the reservation of vengeance to God. “Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord” (Rom 12:19) is not a counsel of resignation but an assignment of jurisdiction, and it is the only answer to a case where the civil remedy failed completely. The dead of Cabrieres got no justice in Provence; the register in Revelation is kept, and the comfort offered to the church in such a case is precisely that God has not forgotten a name of it.

pos: n. (Waldensian valley of the Dauphine above the Durance; object of the crusade of 1487 and 1488)
etymology: French Freissinières, from Occitan fraisse, an ash tree, with the collective ending—the place of ash woods.
biblical_def: The Val Freissinieres is a side valley of the upper Durance in the Dauphine, below Embrun, and with Argentiere and Vallouise it held the French Alpine branch of the Waldensian people. In 1487 Pope Innocent the Eighth published a bull against them and a crusade was preached; the archdeacon Alberto Cattaneo was sent as legate, and with troops raised in Dauphine and Piedmont he went through the valleys in 1487 and 1488. Freissinieres was attacked and its inhabitants driven to the heights; the record of the proceedings, including the interrogations, survived and is one of the best sources for what the Waldensians of the Alps actually believed before the Reformation reached them—that the Scriptures are the rule, that the Roman clergy had no authority to forgive sins, that purgatory and the invocation of saints are inventions, and that their own barbes were their ministers. The valley was not emptied, and its people were still there to join the Reformed churches in the following century. The dictionary enters Freissinieres because the inquisitor's own register is the evidence: the doctrine the Reformation preached in the 1520s was being confessed by Alpine peasants under interrogation in the 1480s.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a crusade as an expedition undertaken with a religious pretext; an inquisitor as an officer of the court of inquisition; and interrogation as the act of questioning.
webster_full: CRUSADE, n. A military expedition undertaken by Christians against infidels or heretics, for the recovery of the Holy Land or the suppression of heresy.
INQUISITOR, n. [L. inquisitor.] One whose official duty it is to inquire; a member of the court of Inquisition.
INTERROGATION, n. [L. interrogatio.] The act of questioning; a question put; examination by questions.
BULL, n. [L. bulla, a seal.] A letter, edict or rescript of the pope, published or transmitted and sealed with lead.
REGISTER, n. A written account of proceedings, preserved as authentic evidence; a book of record.

corruption_summary: Dauphine Waldensian valley attacked in the crusade of 1487, whose inquisition register records its people confessing the rule of Scripture before the Reformation.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the crusade turned inward: the machinery raised for war against the infidel used against the pope's own subjects, with indulgences offered to the troops. It was done against the Hussites and it was done here, against a few thousand farmers in a side valley, and the dictionary names the bull of 1487 as what it was. The second corruption is in the register itself: the clergy whose authority the valley denied were the judges who tried it for denying them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one the register unintentionally proves. “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20) was the Waldensian position in 1487, in the words of illiterate and literate alike under examination. The Reformation was therefore not an innovation of the universities; it was the recovery, by scholars with a printing press, of what hill people had been dying for already.

pos: n. (Dauphine valley above Briancçon, renamed for Louis the Eleventh; a Waldensian valley attacked in 1488)
etymology: French Vallouise, the valley of Louis, renamed in honour of Louis the Eleventh; its earlier name was the Vallis Puta, which the older spelling rendered unflatteringly.
biblical_def: Vallouise is the valley of the Gyronde above Briancon in the Dauphine, and before its renaming in the fifteenth century it was one of the Waldensian valleys of the French Alps. In the campaign of 1488, part of the crusade published the previous year by Innocent the Eighth, the troops under the legate's authority came up the valley and the inhabitants withdrew to the high ground and into the caves above it, as they had done before. This time the troops followed. The account, which comes in substance from the proceedings themselves as well as from the later Protestant historians, is that fires were lit at the mouths of the caves and that those inside, said to have been many score and chiefly women, children and the old, died there. Such of the people as survived conformed or came down from the valley, and Vallouise, unlike Freissinieres, ceased to be a Waldensian place. The dictionary enters it as the plainest answer to a question the valleys raise, which is why the Alpine Waldensians survived in Piedmont and not in Dauphine. They survived where the ground was defensible and the prince was weak, and they were destroyed where it was not, and the difference was not their faith.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a cave as a hollow place in the earth; smothering as the suffocating by excluding air; and extinction as the putting an end to, a destroying utterly.
webster_full: CAVE, n. [L. cavus, hollow.] A hollow place in the earth; a subterraneous cavern; a den.
SMOTHER, v.t. To suffocate or extinguish life by causing smoke or dust to be inhaled, or by excluding air.
EXTINCTION, n. [L. extinctio.] The act of putting out or destroying light or fire; destruction; suppression; a putting an end to.
CONFORM, v.i. To comply with or yield to; to live or act according to, as a rule or an established church.
DEFENSIBLE, adj. That may be defended; capable of being maintained or justified.

corruption_summary: Dauphine valley whose Waldensian people were destroyed in the caves above it in 1488, and which ceased after that to be a Waldensian place.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the completed persecution—the case in which the persecutor wins. The dictionary records it deliberately, because the histories of the valleys are written from the places that survived, and a reader who sees only Angrogna and Torre Pellice may conclude that faithfulness and survival go together. They do not. Vallouise was as faithful as the Val Pellice and it was wiped out, and the difference lay in the gradient of the ground and the strength of the local prince.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that providence is not a reward scheme. “they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth” (Heb 11:38) is said in a chapter which has just distinguished those who escaped the edge of the sword from those who were slain by it, and commends both. “It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed” (Lam 3:22) is the right word in the mouth of a survivor, and it is not an explanation of why the others were.
